'''David Gerald Blair''' (born 26 November 1946) is an Australian physicist and professor at the [[University of Western Australia]] and Director of the Australian International Gravitational Research Centre. Blair works on methods for the detection of [[gravitational wave]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.news.uwa.edu.au/201109133908/international/researchers-new-gravity-measurement-breakthrough |title=Researchers in new gravity measurement breakthrough |publisher=University of Western Australia |accessdate=11 May 2012}}</ref> He developed the [[niobium]] bar gravitational wave detector [[NIOBE]],<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.1908|title = High Sensitivity Gravitational Wave Antenna with Parametric Transducer Readout|journal = Physical Review Letters|volume = 74|issue = 11|pages = 1908–1911|year = 1995|last1 = Blair|first1 = D.|last2 = Ivanov|first2 = E.|last3 = Tobar|first3 = M.|last4 = Turner|first4 = P.|last5 = Van Kann|first5 = F.|last6 = Heng|first6 = I.|pmid = 10057794|bibcode = 1995PhRvL..74.1908B}}</ref> which achieved the lowest observed noise temperature, and participated in a worldwide collaboration that set the best limit on the burst events in 2001. He has been responsible for numerous innovations including the 1984 invention of the first sapphire clock, a super-precise timepiece designed for space, as well as underpinning the research of the Frequency Stability Group at The University of Western Australia.

In 2003, together with [[John Robert de Laeter]], Blair founded the [[Gravity Discovery Centre]], a major centre for the promotion of science in Western Australia.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.gravitycentre.com.au/nggallery/thumbnails |title=The Gravity Discovery Centre Discover a new Universe |access-date=22 December 2014 |archive-url= https://archive.today/20141222053433/http://www.gravitycentre.com.au/nggallery/thumbnails |archive-date=22 December 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2010, Blair and collaborating partners developed an educational research program called the Science Education Enrichment Project,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.seeproject.org.au/ |title=The Science Education Enrichment Project |access-date=22 December 2014 |archive-date=22 December 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141222211437/http://www.seeproject.org.au/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> to research the benefits of specialist exhibition centres such as the Gravity Discovery Centre.  In 2014, Blair led the Einstein-First Project which aims to introduce Einsteinian Physics at an early age. The project partners included Curtin University, Edith Cowan University, Graham (Polly) Farmer Foundation, U.S. Air Force Academy and the Gravity Discovery Centre.

==Early life==
Born in [[Lymington]], Hampshire, England in 1946, Blair emigrated to Australia with his family in 1950.<ref>{{cite web |title=Blair, David Gerald (1946 - ) |url=https://www.eoas.info/biogs/P006174b.htm |website=[[Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Innovation]] |access-date=29 January 2026}}</ref> He received a Bachelor of Science degree from the [[University of Western Australia]] in 1968<ref>{{cite web |title=Convocation - 50th Reunion UWA Graduates 1968 |url=https://www.uwa.edu.au/partners-and-community/-/media/documents/50th-reunion/50th-reunion-booklet-for-the-graduates-of-1968.pdf |publisher=[[University of Western Australia]] |access-date=29 January 2026}}</ref> and a PhD from the [[University of East Anglia]] in 1973, where he investigated [[superfluidity]] in [[liquid helium]].<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=The Australian Physicist |title=Radiophysics, Astrophysics and Gravitation Session - Dr. Blair|page=111 |issue=7 |date=August 1980 |volume=17 |publisher=Australian Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David G. Blair |url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/1016217 |website=[[INSPIRE-HEP]] |access-date=29 January 2026}}</ref>

==Honours and recognition==
Blair was awarded the [[Prime Minister's Prizes for Science#Prime Minister's Prize for Science|Prime Minister's Prize for Science]] in 2020, and received a share - as a contributor - of the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] in 2016.<ref name="uwa">{{cite web |title=David Blair |url=https://research-repository.uwa.edu.au/en/persons/david-blair/prizes/ |publisher=[[University of Western Australia]] |access-date=29 January 2026}}</ref> He received the [[RSWA Medal]] from the [[Royal Society of Western Australia]] in 2018,<ref>{{cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.rswa.org.au/royal-society-medal/past-recipients/ |website=[[Royal Society of Western Australia]] |access-date=29 January 2026}}</ref> the [[Australian and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science#ANZAAS Medal|ANZAAS Medal]] from the [[Australian and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2005,<ref name="uwa"/> the [[Eureka Prizes|Eureka Prize]] for Promoting Understanding of Science in 2005,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://eureka.australianmuseum.net.au/7537F9BD-EB56-2006-84C9841C04AA1401 |title=Eureka Prizes: 2005 Winner |publisher=Australian Museum |access-date=10 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315093231/http://eureka.australianmuseum.net.au/7537F9BD-EB56-2006-84C9841C04AA1401 |archive-date=15 March 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the [[Walter Boas Medal]] from the [[Australian Institute of Physics]] in 1995.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aip.org.au/content/boas |title=Walter Boas Medal |publisher=Australian Institute of Physics |accessdate=11 May 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120317120246/http://www.aip.org.au/content/boas |archivedate=17 March 2012 |df=dmy-all }}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2013, and a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/fellowship/fellows/emeritus-professor-david-blair|title=Emeritus Professor David Blair {{!}} Australian Academy of Science|website=science.org.au|access-date=2018-06-16}}</ref> Blair was appointed an [[Order of Australia|Officer of the Order of Australia]] in the [[2026 King's Birthday Honours (Australia)|2026 King's Birthday Honours]] in recognition of "distinguished service to physics, to precision measurement science, to gravitational wave research, and to scientific education".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor David Gerald Blair |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/3077434 |access-date=2026-06-07 |website=Australian Honours Search Facility}}</ref>

==Publications==
Blair is the co-author of ''Ripples on a Cosmic Sea: The Search for Gravitational Waves'',<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LKyGuN1qveAC |title=Ripples on a Cosmic Sea: The Search for Gravitational Waves |accessdate=11 May 2012|isbn=9780738201375 |last1=Blair |first1=David |last2=McNamara |first2=Geoff |date=7 April 1999 |publisher=Basic Books }}</ref> and the editor of the book ''The Detection of Gravitational Waves''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blair |first1=David |title=The detection of gravitational waves |date=2005 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=9780511600104 |edition=Digitally printed first paperback version |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/detection-of-gravitational-waves/4840FA275A002D3F5D271512DDB8C5CC |access-date=21 December 2025}}</ref>

He has also written a science fiction novel about a post-apocalytic Earth where contact is made to a galactic community via the essentially one-way communication starstream network.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blair |first1=David |title=Starstream |date=2023 |publisher=Amazon Kindle Edition |isbn=9781922781079 |url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/Starstream-David-Blair-ebook/dp/B0BYK9P4SG |access-date=21 December 2025}}</ref> Faster than light travel or communication is assumed to be impossible, in accord with current scientific theories.
